title: Why Does My Puppy Keep Chewing Everything?
description: Wondering why your puppy chews everything in sight? Here is what drives it, how long it tends to last, and how to protect your home and your sanity.
excerpt: Chewing is how puppies explore, soothe sore gums and burn off energy, and with a few smart habits you can get through it.
seoTitle: Why Does My Puppy Keep Chewing Everything?
imageAlt: Golden retriever puppy resting its head on its paws
midImageAlt: Golden retriever puppy sitting on green grass
quick: Puppies chew because they explore with their mouths, because teething makes their gums sore, and because boredom or extra energy builds up. It is normal and usually eases between six months and a year. Manage the space, offer safe chews, and calmly redirect your puppy to something they are allowed to chew.

faq.q: How long does puppy chewing last?
faq.a: For most puppies, the heaviest chewing eases somewhere between six months and a year, as teething finishes and energy settles. Some puppies calm down sooner and others keep chewing longer, especially if they are bored or under-exercised. Steady supervision, good chews and enough rest help a lot. If the destruction is still heavy after a year, talk with your vet or a trainer.

faq.q: Is it normal for my puppy to chew everything?
faq.a: Yes, very much so. Chewing is how puppies explore, cope with teething and burn off energy, and it is one of the most common things new owners ask about. It does not mean your puppy is naughty or that you have failed. It does mean that anything within reach is fair game, so the most useful thing you can do is manage the space and keep good chews on hand.

faq.q: What can I give my puppy to chew on?
faq.a: Choose chew toys sized for your puppy and made for dogs, and check them regularly for pieces that come loose. Rotate toys so they stay interesting, and supervise any chew until you know how your puppy handles it. Avoid anything small enough to swallow. If you are unsure which chews suit your puppy's size and age, ask your veterinarian.

faq.q: Should I be worried if my puppy swallows something?
faq.a: Yes, take it seriously. If you think your puppy has swallowed something that is not food, or you notice vomiting, loss of appetite, straining or unusual tiredness, contact your veterinarian promptly rather than waiting to see whether it passes. If you can, keep the packaging or a photo of the item, because your vet will want to know what it was and roughly how much.

faq.q: Does chewing mean my puppy is bored?
faq.a: Sometimes, but not always. Boredom is one common cause, alongside teething and plain curiosity. A puppy who chews heavily late in the day, after a busy morning, or when left alone for long stretches may be under-stimulated or anxious. Try short training sessions, a puzzle feeder and a quiet rest period. If the pattern continues, look at the whole day rather than one single cause.

faq.q: How do I stop my puppy chewing furniture?
faq.a: Start with management. Block access with a gate or closed door, use the crate or a playpen when you cannot watch, and keep valuables off low surfaces. When you catch your puppy chewing furniture, calmly move them to a chew they are allowed and praise them for taking it. Avoid scolding, since it often teaches a puppy to chew when you are out of sight. Consistent redirection over several weeks usually works better than any single trick.

html:
It is 6:40 on a Sunday morning and you are on your hands and knees looking for the second slipper. The first one is in the hallway, chewed into something resembling soggy lace. Your puppy is sitting beside you with a wagging tail, looking extremely pleased with the whole arrangement. So why does my puppy keep chewing things? The short answer is that chewing is how young puppies explore the world, soothe sore gums and burn off energy. It is normal, it is usually temporary, and most of it can be managed without drama.

The longer answer comes down to three main drivers: exploring, teething, and boredom or excess energy. Often more than one is at work at the same time. The good news is that you do not have to stop the chewing altogether. You need to point it toward things that are fine to chew, and make the wrong things harder to reach. Every puppy is different, so think of the timeline below as a rough guide rather than a promise.

The mouth is a puppy's hands

Think about how a toddler explores. Everything goes in the mouth. Puppies do the same, except their mouths are full of sharp little teeth. A new puppy does not yet know which things matter to you. A sock, a TV remote, the corner of the rug and a dropped crisp are all just interesting textures and smells. That is the real answer to the question of why puppies chew on everything: everything is new, and their mouths are how they check it out.

Chewing also helps puppies make sense of their surroundings. A chewed-up slipper is often less of a plan to ruin your morning and more of a puppy asking what this thing is and how it feels. Expect a lot of this in the first few weeks, when the whole house is still a mystery to them.

Teething, and what it feels like from the inside

Puppies start with baby teeth, which fall out and make way for adult teeth. Roughly between three and six months is when much of that change happens, and it can leave gums tender and itchy. Chewing feels good, so your puppy will go looking for things to bite down on. Teething timing varies from puppy to puppy, so treat that window as a general pattern rather than a schedule.

Watch for signs such as more chewing than usual, some drooling, a few spots of blood on a toy, or a puppy who seems to chew on cold things just to soothe their mouth. Those are normal. If gums look very swollen or bleeding, or your puppy stops eating, call your veterinarian. The RSPCA's puppy care advice is a helpful place to read more about general puppy health and what to expect as your puppy grows.

When boredom and extra energy are the real problem

A puppy who is bored, overtired or wound up tends to chew in a more determined way. Picture the cushion that gets shredded at five in the afternoon. That puppy often had a busy morning with too much excitement and a nap that never quite happened. Puppies need a lot more sleep than most new owners expect, and an overtired puppy can look like a tiny tornado.

Chewing can also be a stress outlet. Some puppies struggle when they are left alone, and the chewing starts to look like a coping strategy. The Dogs Trust guidance on helping a dog get used to time alone is worth a read if the chewing happens mostly when you walk out the door. If you work full time, our piece on a puppy schedule when you work full time can help you plan the day around breaks, play and rest.

How long this phase tends to last

Most people want a clear answer to the puppy chewing how long does it last question, and the honest answer is that it depends on the puppy. Here is a rough picture of what many puppies go through:

AgeWhat is usually going onWhat tends to help
8 to 10 weeksEverything is new and the mouth is the main toolClose supervision, a few good chews, lots of short naps
10 to 12 weeksCuriosity peaks and attention spans are shortPuppy-proofed rooms and regular short play sessions
3 to 4 monthsBaby teeth start falling out and gums feel soreCold chews you can supervise and rotating toys
4 to 6 monthsAdult teeth come through and chewing can feel more intenseA steady routine, more exercise and brain games, and chews always within reach

8 to 10 weeks

At this age your puppy is still settling in. Many first nights are noisy, and the chewing often starts as soon as you stop watching. Use a crate or playpen for stretches when you cannot supervise, and keep the rest of the house tidy. Our guide to crate training a puppy explains how to make the crate a calm, safe place rather than a punishment.

10 to 12 weeks

Curiosity is at a high point and focus is short. This is when people often notice that every shoe in the house has teeth marks. Short play sessions, a few changes of toy and plenty of sleep usually make a bigger difference than any single rule.

3 to 4 months

Teething often becomes obvious now. Keep a small selection of cold or chilled chews for supervised use, and expect the chewing to come in waves. Some days will feel fine and others will feel like a setback. Both are normal.

4 to 6 months

Adult teeth are arriving and many puppies become more confident and more energetic at the same time. This is a common age for chewing to intensify. A consistent routine, more daily exercise that suits your puppy's age, and gentle brain games can help. Keep the good chews within reach so your puppy has somewhere to go.

Many puppies noticeably improve somewhere around six months to a year, though some keep a chewing habit into adulthood, especially if they are bored. If the destruction is still heavy after a year, that is worth a conversation with your veterinarian or a trainer.

Puppy-proofing the rooms you actually use

Before you can redirect chewing, you have to make the wrong things less available. Get down on the floor and look at the room from puppy height. You will spot things you missed from standing height. Common trouble spots include:

  • Electrical cords, phone chargers and extension leads
  • Shoes, socks and anything with a strap or a lace
  • Remote controls, glasses and small household objects
  • Bins, laundry baskets and anything that smells of food
  • Children's toys, which look just like puppy toys to a puppy
  • Houseplants, which should be checked with your vet before they come within reach

Our new puppy checklist covers the wider set-up if you are still getting your home ready. A puppy-proofed room does not need to look like a nursery. It just needs to be a place where a chewed item is an unlikely event rather than a daily one.

Furniture, shoes and the things you love most

Chewed furniture is one of the most common complaints, and it is understandable. Table legs, sofa corners and skirting boards can look irresistible to a teething puppy. Some puppies go for wood, some for fabric, and some go for whatever you most recently put down. Every puppy is different, so there is no single product or trick that works for all of them.

The most reliable approach is management. Use a gate or closed door to keep your puppy out of rooms where furniture is at risk, and keep a crate or playpen available for times you cannot watch. Put valuable items on higher surfaces. A determined puppy can find a gap, so supervise when you can, and expect a few mistakes while the habit is still forming. Each mistake is information about where your management needs to improve.

Safe chews that hold up

Chewing is not a problem to eliminate. It is a need to meet well. The best chews are sized for your puppy, made for dogs, and checked regularly for damage. A few options many owners use include:

  • Rubber chew toys that are firm enough to last and large enough that they cannot be swallowed
  • Puzzle toys or stuffed chews that you can fill with a small amount of your puppy's own food
  • Cold, damp cloths or chilled chews that you supervise, which many teething puppies find soothing
  • A rotating set of toys, so the box does not become boring within a week

Be careful with rope toys, which can fray, and with anything that splinters or breaks into small pieces. Supervise any new chew until you know how your puppy handles it. A chew that a puppy finishes in ten minutes is one they will finish in ten minutes, so the goal is a mix of quick and longer-lasting options. Our puppy essentials list includes a simple starter set of supplies if you are still building your stash.

Redirect and reward, one step at a time

Redirecting is the heart of the approach. It teaches your puppy what is fine to chew through positive reinforcement, which is the only method we recommend. Here is a simple routine you can use:

  1. Keep a suitable chew nearby whenever you cannot watch your puppy closely, and keep one in your hand when you are sitting on the sofa together.
  2. When you notice your puppy starting to chew something they should not, calmly interrupt with a quiet word or a gentle movement, and take the item out of reach.
  3. Offer an approved chew straight away and let your puppy take it, without any scolding or drama.
  4. As soon as your puppy starts chewing the right thing, praise them warmly and give a treat or a quiet bit of fuss.
  5. Make the swap easy: keep the approved chews where your puppy spends time, and keep the forbidden items out of reach.
  6. Expect progress to be uneven. Keep going for several weeks rather than judging it by a single bad afternoon.

Scolding and punishing do not work well here. A puppy who is told off often learns to chew when you are out of sight, or to hide what they have done, which is not what you want. If your puppy also nips or mouths at hands, our article on how to stop puppy biting covers that behaviour in more detail. The ASPCA's guidance on mouthing and biting in puppies is also useful reading.

When to ask a professional

Most chewing is a normal part of puppyhood, but a few situations need a professional. Contact your veterinarian straight away if you think your puppy has swallowed something that is not food, or if you notice vomiting, straining, a swollen belly, a sudden loss of appetite or unusual lethargy. Do not wait to see whether an item passes if you suspect your puppy has swallowed something. Your vet can advise on what to do next.

Also speak with your vet if your puppy's gums look very swollen or bleed, or if your puppy stops eating, because these can be signs of something other than normal teething. If the chewing is causing heavy destruction, injuries or seems linked to anxiety when you leave, a qualified trainer or behaviourist can help you build a plan around your puppy's needs. Every puppy is different, and getting extra support early is nothing to feel bad about.
